title: On Measuring Unnoticeability of Graph Adversarial Attacks: Observations, New Measure, and Applications

problem.claim: Graph adversarial attacks are treated as allegedly unnoticeable.

gap.claim: Existing graph attack-noticeability measures have critical limitations: attackers can bypass simple rules while maintaining attack performance, and global statistics may overlook attacks until severe perturbations occur.

contributions.claim: The authors identify two critical limitations in existing graph attack-noticeability measures.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph adversarial attacks are allegedly unnoticeable.
Prior measures primarily use statistical tests comparing the topology of original and potentially attacked graphs.
The existing measures are reported to have two critical limitations.
Simple-rule measures can be bypassed while attack performance is maintained, and global-statistic measures can miss attacks until severe perturbations occur.

source_observation.claim: Noticeability measures based on simple rules can be bypassed without reducing attack performance.

interpretation.claim: A measure may fail to reflect attack effectiveness when its detection rule is directly optimizable by the attacker.

application.claim: Assess adversarial-attack noticeability measures against adaptive attacks that target the measure itself.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this limitation applies to every simple-rule measure or attack setting.

source_observation.claim: Measures based on global statistics such as degree distributions may overlook attacks until severe perturbations occur.

interpretation.claim: Global aggregate statistics may be insensitive to localized or structurally subtle perturbations.

application.claim: Evaluate noticeability using statistics that can detect relevant structural changes before severe perturbations occur.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify which alternative statistics or perturbation regimes would address this limitation.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the proposed new measure.
No datasets, experimental setup, quantitative results, or comparisons are provided.
The abstract does not identify the applications of the work.
